description: We are a motivated team passionate about space, science, technology, and solving real-world problems. We bring different skills and ideas together to create innovative solutions. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we want to learn, challenge ourselves, and use NASA’s data and resources to build something creative and meaningful.
summary:
Mars Analog Finder is a free web app that finds places on Earth whose terrain resembles a chosen spot on Mars, or the other way round. It compares 16 spots in Jezero crater, where NASA’s Perseverance rover landed, with about 240 land squares, each 10 km across, in 16 regions on Earth: deserts plus classic Mars analog sites such as the Antarctic Dry Valleys, Iceland’s highlands and Devon Island. For each square it measures slope, height range, roughness and curvature from NASA, USGS and Copernicus data, adds an iron comparison from Mars Odyssey gamma-ray maps, and leaves out sea and lakes. A small model, trained on 86 Mars–Earth pairs our team labelled, turns those measurements into the chance a person would call two places alike. On pairs it hadn’t seen, it ranked them better than hand-set scoring (0.91 against 0.78). Users can pick a place or type coordinates, see both places side by side, and read why they match.

Scientists test rovers and instruments at Earth analog sites, usually chosen from a few well-known places. Our tool gives a fast, transparent shortlist across many regions and shows students how planetary comparisons are made.
details:
Our tool identifies and characterizes new terrestrial analogs for a real Mars landing site. We start from Jezero crater, where Perseverance landed, and measure the terrain properties that landing-site selection depends on (average slope, steepest slopes, roughness, curvature, and height range) the same way on Mars and Earth. We do this using data from NASA's Mars Odyssey and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, as well as ESA's Copernicus Sentinel-2.

We compare these Mars metrics with about 240 land squares across 16 Earth regions, including deserts, the Antarctic Dry Valleys, Devon Island’s Haughton crater, and volcanic terrain in Iceland, Hawaii, and Arizona. A model, trained on pairs labeled by our team, ranks the matches and explains them. Beyond well-known sites, it points to less-studied candidates such as parts of the Namib and Libyan deserts, while a known analog near Erfoud, Morocco, ranks highly as a check on our method. Everything is presented in a public web tool with maps, side-by-side views, and a search that works from Mars to Earth or the reverse.

What it does and how it works Mars Analog Finder is a free web app that finds places on Earth whose terrain resembles a chosen spot on Mars, and vice versa. Users start from a place on either planet, pick it from a list or type its coordinates, and get a ranked list of the closest matches on the other planet.

  1. Matching squares: Mars and Earth are cut into 10 km squares and measured the same way. The Mars side has 16 spots in Jezero crater, while the Earth side has about 240 land squares in 16 regions (deserts, dry plateaus, plus five classic Mars analog sites).
  2. Measurements: Each square is evaluated for average slope, steepest slopes, height range, roughness, curvature, and image texture. Both planets share one scale, so a number means the same thing on Mars and Earth.
  3. A learned score: A lightweight model—trained on 86 Mars–Earth pairs our team labeled as alike or different—turns the measurements into the probability that a person would call the two places alike.
  4. Iron comparison: Mars iron from Mars Odyssey gamma-ray maps is compared with an Earth iron-oxide proxy by ranking each place against its own planet, neutralizing the issue of different measurement units.
  5. Explanations: Each match is shown side-by-side with the starting place as a shaded relief under the same lighting. The app lists which measurements agree and differ, and charts both places on the shared scale.

Benefits

  • Accessible: Free and open, with no account or installation required. Built entirely from public NASA, USGS, and Copernicus data. Works on both desktop and mobile devices.
  • Transparent: Every match explains itself, and the "About" tab shows exactly what the model learned and how uncertain its results are.
  • Honest: If a typed location is outside the data, at sea, or on water, the app says so and names the nearest covered place instead of inventing an answer.

Intended impact Scientists and mission planners test rovers, instruments, and procedures at Earth analog sites, usually chosen from a few well-known places. This tool provides a fast, data-backed shortlist across many regions, pointing researchers to new sites worth investigating. It also serves as an educational tool, letting students see exactly how planetary comparisons are made and how measurement, labeling, and testing work in a real AI project.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Language: Python 3.13
  • Libraries: NumPy and SciPy (calculations), pandas (tables), rasterio and PROJ (Mars map projections), Altair (charts), and Streamlit (web app).
  • Earth data: Google Earth Engine with Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery and the Copernicus 30 m elevation model. (Near the poles, only summer images are used).
  • Mars data: USGS Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX elevation mosaic (20 m), USGS Mars 2020 CTX image mosaic (6 m), and NASA Mars Odyssey Gamma Ray Spectrometer element maps (Planetary Data System).
  • Analog sites: Catalogue of Planetary Analogues (Open University, for ESA).
  • AI model: A single-neuron logistic regression written from scratch with SciPy, plus our own labeling page and training tool.
  • Testing and hosting: pytest (77 automated tests), Git/GitHub, and Streamlit Community Cloud.
  • Hardware/Compute: A Windows laptop; satellite processing ran on Google’s cloud.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped write some code. The team ran, tested, labeled, debugged, and verified everything manually.

How it’s creative

  • Two-way planetary search: You can start from Mars or Earth, and our tests confirm a pair gets the exact same score in both directions.
  • One ruler for two planets: Both planets are measured and scaled together. Iron is compared by rank so that differing units don’t break the comparison.
  • Custom, verified AI: The labeling sheet hides the app’s scores, so ground-truth labels come entirely from human judgment. Testing leaves out a whole pair at a time and reports a likely range. On unseen pairs, our learned model scored 0.91 (likely 0.82 to 0.97) against 0.78 (0.68 to 0.88) for hand-set weights, proving a +0.13 improvement.
  • Active learning: New label sheets prioritize pairs the model is least sure about, maximizing what it learns from each new label.
  • Reporting failures: We tested six extra landform measurements that didn't improve the model, so we creatively chose to keep it simpler and faster rather than bloated.

Factors our team considered

  • Data limits: The Mars side currently covers only the middle of Jezero crater because the matching image covers less ground than the elevation data. Iron maps are 5° cells (about 300 km across). Furthermore, the Earth elevation model includes buildings and trees, which we had to account for.
  • Comparing different instruments: Mars and Earth images come from different cameras. Our model successfully learned to give image texture zero weight, relying purely on slope and curvature instead.
  • Fair testing: Hand-set scoring was kept unchanged as a baseline. We report results with likely ranges and only claim a method is better when the entire range is above zero.
  • Label bias: Labels came from our team, not independent experts. Labellers were instructed to judge land shape rather than color, meaning the model's behavior directly reflects this specific instruction.
  • Terrain filtering: Vegetated land, seas, and lakes are filtered out automatically. Polar squares may still include glacier ice, so an ice-check using Sentinel-2’s short-wave infrared band is actively being built next.
  • Licensing and safety: The app and README carry required Copernicus attribution, cite USGS/NASA datasets, and credit the analog catalogue. The public app loads data in a safe format that cannot execute code, and no passwords or API keys are exposed in the project.
